title: Handover, competency and specialist referrals
audience: Any worker in any home-service business in the academy, working under supervision.
learningOutcomes: Explain the boundary for handover, competency and specialist referrals and identify when work must stop.
Prepare a task-specific, documented decision for handover, competency and specialist referrals under company and local requirements.

instruction.heading: Why close-out and referral matter
instruction.body: A job is not finished when the last cloth is put away. It is finished when the authorised work has been completed and recorded, the work that was not authorised has been excluded and reported, and the next person knows what they can and cannot do. This lesson covers three linked decisions: the handover of completed work to the client or site, the check that the worker is competent for the task being signed off, and the referral of tasks, hazards or claims that belong to a specialist. Each one needs a clear record. Without it, a client may later believe that work was done that was not, or that a site is safe when nobody checked.

instruction.heading: Write an accurate handover
instruction.body: A handover states what was done, where, with which products and methods, and when. It also states what was not done and why, such as an area excluded because the material was uncharacterised, a stain left untreated because its cause was unknown, or a repair outside the cleaning scope. Record any residual condition you observed, such as damage that was present before the work or a surface that was unsuitable for the method. Use plain, factual language, and avoid words that imply certainty you do not have. Before-and-after photographs, where the site allows them, support the record. The client should receive a copy or summary and the chance to ask questions before the job is closed.

instruction.heading: Decline unsupported certification
instruction.body: Clients sometimes ask a cleaner to certify that a site is clean, safe, decontaminated or free of a hazard. A cleaning business should not give that certification unless it holds a qualified person's evidence for it and the certification is within its authority. Where a client asks for it on a site you could not assess, decline the certificate, report only the observed and authorised work, and refer the certification question to an appropriately qualified specialist. Write the reason in the record.

instruction.heading: Check competency before sign-off
instruction.body: A worker signs off a task only when they are competent for that task and the method used. Competency is shown by a combination of records: the training completed, the supervised tasks signed off by a competent person, and a practical verification of the specific method. A training certificate is evidence of training, not proof of current competence for a specific task. Check that the worker has performed the method under supervision, that the record is current, and that any licence the work requires is held by the person who did it. Where a worker is not verified, the sign-off belongs to a verified person, and the record must show who signed off what. Review competency records when equipment, products or methods change.

instruction.heading: Refer what is outside the approved scope
instruction.body: Refer a task or hazard to a specialist when it is outside the worker's training or the business's authority, when the material or hazard is unidentified, when the work needs a licence the business does not hold, or when the client wants a result the approved method cannot give. A referral is a written handover to a specialist with the facts: the site, the request, what was observed, what was reported, what was done, what remains unknown, and any photographs or product information you hold. Record the referral with the person it went to and the date. The cleaning job is either held or closed with the excluded work stated, and the client is told who will take over that work. Do not give an opinion you are not qualified to give, and do not pass on a claim you could not verify.

instruction.heading: Worked example on an unknown site
instruction.body: Consider a client who asks, at handover, for a certificate that a site is fully decontaminated. The site had an unknown contamination history. The cleaner's record shows what was cleaned, with which approved products, and what was not assessed. The cleaner declines the certificate, explains that the business cannot verify the decontamination status of the site, and refers the certification question in writing to a qualified specialist. The handover says that the observed cleaning was completed and that decontamination was not assessed.

instruction.heading: Licence notice
instruction.body: Licence notice: This lesson does not grant any licence, certificate or authority to perform regulated work, and it does not qualify a worker to sign off licensed work. Check the licence rules where the work takes place, and make the referral to a provider who holds the relevant authority.

instruction.heading: Stop-work rule
instruction.body: Stop, refer and tell your supervisor if you are asked to sign off a task you did not perform or are not verified to perform, if the client asks you to certify a condition you cannot verify, if the record would be incomplete without the excluded work being stated, or if a hazard is found after the handover has been drafted. Do not close the job until the record matches the work done.

procedure: Confirm that the work completed matches the accepted scope and the work order.
List any work not performed, with the reason, and any residual condition or damage observed.
Record the products, methods, times, photographs where allowed, and the people present.
Check the competency record of each person who signed off a task, and confirm that their training, supervision and verification are current.
Decline any certification the evidence does not support, and state why in the record.
Refer any excluded, unidentified or licensed work in writing to an appropriately authorised specialist, with the facts you hold.
Give the client a clear handover that states what was done, what was excluded and who will take over the excluded work.
File the handover, the competency record and the referral together with the job.

workedExamples.situation: The client requests a certificate stating that an unknown site is fully decontaminated.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What is the first safe action, and who must be told?
workedExamples.reasoning: The first safe action is not to sign the certificate. Record what was cleaned and what was not assessed, then tell the client in writing that the business cannot certify decontamination. Refer the question to a qualified specialist, and record the referral and its date. Do not describe the site as safe in any handover or conversation.

workedExamples.situation: The site requests sign-off for a hazard outside the approved work order.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Can the cleaner sign off the hazard as cleared?
workedExamples.reasoning: No. The hazard is outside the approved work order, so the cleaner did not assess it and is not authorised to clear it. Record that it was observed, do not sign it off, and inform the site contact in writing. Refer the hazard to the person who holds authority over the site and to a specialist, and state in the handover that the hazard remains open.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Licence notice: completing this lesson is not a licence, certificate or authority to do regulated or restricted work. Check the licence or authorisation rules for your state or territory, and obtain your employer or site written authorisation before starting any work that is outside your training.

Stop-work rule: stop, make the area safe and tell your supervisor before continuing if the task is outside your training or authorisation, the hazard or the required permission is unclear, or the client asks for work that the work order does not cover.

qualityStandard: The handover account covers the completed tasks, the scope carved out, and the open unknowns, and it avoids certifying any state the evidence cannot back.
A training certificate is not treated as proof of current competence, and sign-off requires supervised and verified performance.
Unidentified, unauthorised or licensed work is referred in writing to an appropriately authorised specialist.
The handover, the competency record and the referral are filed together with the job.
summary: The handover records the work completed, the work excluded, and the matters still unresolved.
Do not sign or certify a condition that the evidence does not support.
A training certificate is evidence of training; competence for a task needs supervised and verified performance.
Refer unidentified, unauthorised or licensed work in writing to an appropriately authorised specialist.
Keep the handover, the competency record and the referral together with the job.
This lesson does not grant any licence, certificate or authority to perform or sign off regulated work.

knowledgeChecks.question: Before starting work classified as "Handover, competency and specialist referrals", what must you do?
options: Start the work and check hazards as you go, since the client has asked for it and the client has paid a deposit
Identify task-specific unknown hazards, qualifications, permissions and controls; place work on hold until verified.
Accept the task if your past experience with similar jobs was safe and the client has been clear about what they want
Ask the client to sign a waiver so the work can begin and the waiver covers every hazard on site

knowledgeChecks.question: Can a worker be handed restricted work once a training certificate is filed with the employer?
options: Yes, once the training certificate has been filed with the employer and the client has agreed to the job
Yes, if the client agrees in writing and the client pays a deposit up front for the job
No. Relevant licences, employer/site authorisation and independent competence verification remain required.
Only if the work is outdoors and at ground level and the work is short, simple and low risk

knowledgeChecks.question: Is a training certificate proof of current competence for a specific method?
options: No, it is evidence of training, not proof of current competence for a specific method
